title: The Society of Jesus (1540)
hookLine: seven friends at Paris become an order, for the greater glory of God

cards: Ignatius is back in school. In Paris he sits in class, older than the students around him, starting again from the basics. He has decided that to help people, he needs to study.

At the university he shares rooms with two younger men, Pierre Favre and Francis Xavier. One by one, a small band of friends gathers around him. On a hill above Paris, at Montmartre, they make vows together.
They don't yet know they're founding anything. The world will end up calling them Jesuits.

teach.h: THE PLAN THAT FAILED: NO SHIP.
teach.b: First, the plan that failed. The friends meant to go to Jerusalem and live where Jesus lived. They waited in Venice for a ship, and no pilgrim ship sailed.
So they turned to their backup plan: go to Rome and offer themselves to the pope, to be sent wherever he thought best. A failed plan set the shape of everything after. Second, the name.
When people asked who they were, they answered: the Company of Jesus, since they had no head but him. In Latin, the Society of Jesus.
Pope Paul the Third approved them as a religious order, and Jesuit is the everyday name that stuck.
Third, the motto: Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, for the greater glory of God. Not glory. Greater glory.

The question is always comparative: of the choices in front of me, which serves God more? It echoes Paul, in the Douay-Rheims: "whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God." Fourth, the habit of mind.
These weren't monks behind walls. They went where they were sent: schools, ports, courts, slums, mission lands.
Ignatius asked them to find God in all things, not only in chapel.
Over the centuries the Jesuits have been praised, feared, opposed, even suppressed for a time and then restored, with admirers and critics inside the Church and out. The motto hasn't changed.
Some Catholic students still write the letters A, M, D, G at the top of their schoolwork.

how: Jesuits and students in Jesuit schools often write AMDG, for Ad maiorem Dei gloriam, at the top of their work, and some Catholics begin the day with a morning offering of everything they'll do.

games.q: you and your friends have vowed to go to Jerusalem. you wait in Venice, and no ship sails. what do you do?
o: keep waiting, however long it takes.
go to Rome and offer yourselves to the pope, to go wherever he sends you.
games.why: they went to Rome. the backup plan became the shape of the order: ready to be sent anywhere.

practice: Picture the rest of your day all at once: the work, the conversations, the errands, the boring parts. If you pray, offer the whole day to God, in your own words or with Paul's: whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God.
If you don't, choose one thing ahead of you and decide to do it as well as you can, for something bigger than you.

wordCard.voice: Jesuit. A member of the Society of Jesus, the order Ignatius and his friends founded, sent wherever the need is greater, for the greater glory of God.

orig.note: Latin: for the greater glory of God, the Jesuit motto, often shortened to AMDG.

carryVoice: Your line: for the greater glory. Not just good, but which serves more. Day eight hundred forty-nine.
